summary: Older tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) that can treat major depression and sometimes anxiety/panic, but it’s a heavier med—more sedation, more anticholinergic side effects, and real cardiac safety considerations.
description: Imipramine is a tricyclic antidepressant that can help major depression and, in some cases, panic symptoms. It tends to be more sedating and more “body side effects” than newer antidepressants—dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, dizziness, and orthostatic hypotension are common. It can affect heart rhythm, so baseline risk checks and sometimes an ECG matter—especially at higher doses or in older adults. Like all antidepressants, it carries an FDA boxed warning about increased suicidal thinking/behavior in people 24 and younger during early treatment and dose changes. It’s generally not a first-choice antidepressant today, but it still has a role when other treatments fail or when a clinician is targeting a specific symptom cluster.
patient_summary: Imipramine is a tricyclic antidepressant that can help major depression and sometimes panic symptoms, but it’s not a “light” medication. Expect more sedation and more side effects like dry mouth, constipation, and dizziness—plus potential heart rhythm issues at higher doses. It also carries the antidepressant boxed warning about increased suicidal thinking/behavior in people 24 and younger early in treatment and during dose changes. It’s usually not first-line today, but it can be useful in specific cases when other meds haven’t worked.

primary.context: A tricyclic antidepressant option for unipolar major depression. Often reserved for cases where first-line antidepressants (SSRIs/SNRIs) haven’t worked or aren’t tolerated, due to side effect burden and safety monitoring needs.

secondary.context: Sometimes dosed at bedtime because it can be sedating. It’s not a dedicated sleep medication, and sedation comes with tradeoffs (next-day grogginess, dizziness, falls).

off_label.context: May be used off-label for panic symptoms in select patients. Symptom improvement typically builds over weeks (not hours), and side effects/heart-risk considerations limit use compared with SSRIs/SNRIs.

therapeutic_response.display: Depression: early effects 1-2 weeks; fuller benefit 4-6 weeks. Panic/anxiety: early effects ~2 weeks, continued improvement 4-6 weeks (sometimes longer).

common_adverse_effects.effect: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary hesitancy)
common_adverse_effects.notes: This medication can feel “drying.” Dry mouth and constipation are the classics. Mild urinary hesitancy can happen. Severe constipation, severe blurry vision, or trouble urinating are red flags—don’t ignore them.
Imipramine can be very sedating—especially early and after dose increases. Bedtime dosing can help, but next-day grogginess is real for some people.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Frequency not defined (risk is high relative to many antidepressants)
common_adverse_effects.notes: If you feel lightheaded standing up, take it seriously. This is one of the main reasons TCAs can be dangerous in older adults (falls).
Some people feel more anxious or keyed up early on (especially during titration). If you notice panic, agitation, or insomnia ramping up hard, reach out—sometimes the plan needs adjusting.
Libido can go down (or sometimes up). Erectile dysfunction can occur. If it’s affecting your quality of life, there are options—don’t suffer in silence.

serious_risks.risk: Cardiac arrhythmias, conduction problems, or severe palpitations (higher risk with heart disease, higher doses, or overdose).
Severe orthostatic hypotension leading to falls or fainting.
Seizures (especially in overdose or in patients with seizure risk).
Severe confusion, hallucinations, or delirium (risk increases in older adults and with anticholinergic burden).
Suicidal ideation/behavior changes early in treatment or during dose adjustments (boxed warning focus).
Serotonin syndrome (especially with other serotonergic medications).
Blood dyscrasias (rare): seek evaluation for fever/sore throat and consider CBC if symptomatic.
Pathological neutrophil depression: discontinue if hematologic toxicity emerges.

safety.black_box_warning: Antidepressants increased the risk compared with placebo of suicidal thinking and behavior (suicidality) in short-term studies in children, adolescents, and young adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) and other psychiatric disorders. Patients of all ages who are started on antidepressant therapy should be monitored appropriately and observed closely for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual changes in behavior. Families and caregivers should be advised of the need for close observation and communication with the health care provider. Imipramine is not approved for use in pediatric patients except for patients with nocturnal enuresis.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to imipramine or any component of the formulation
Acute recovery period after a myocardial infarction (MI)
Use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) intended to treat psychiatric disorders (concurrently or within 14 days of discontinuing either imipramine or the MAOI)
Initiation in patients receiving IV methylene blue

precautions: Cardiac risk: Imipramine can affect heart conduction and rhythm. Risk is higher with preexisting heart disease, higher doses, overdose, and in older adults.
Orthostatic hypotension: Standing up can cause a major blood pressure drop—dizziness, falls, fainting (especially early or with dose increases).
Strong anticholinergic effects: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention—can become medically significant.
Sedation and impaired alertness: Can impair driving and decision-making, especially during initiation and titration.
Seizure risk: Use caution in anyone with seizure history or medications/substances that lower seizure threshold.
Mania/hypomania risk: Like other antidepressants, can trigger mania/hypomania in bipolar disorder—screen before starting.
Serotonin syndrome: Risk increases when combined with other serotonergic meds; watch for agitation, confusion, fever, tremor, rigidity, diarrhea.

interactions.interactant: MAOIs (psychiatric MAOIs; also IV methylene blue)
interactions.mechanism: Contraindicated. High risk of severe adverse reactions including serotonin toxicity and dangerous instability.
interactions.action: Allow 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting imipramine, and 14 days between stopping imipramine and starting an MAOI.

interactions.interactant: Other serotonergic medications (SSRIs/SNRIs, triptans, tramadol, fentanyl, lithium, buspirone, St. John’s wort, tryptophan)
interactions.mechanism: Increased risk of serotonin syndrome (agitation, confusion, fever, tremor/rigidity, diarrhea, seizures).
interactions.action: Use cautiously and monitor closely. Educate patients on warning signs. Stop and seek urgent care if symptoms appear.

interactions.interactant: CYP2D6 inhibitors (e.g., some SSRIs like fluoxetine/paroxetine; bupropion)
interactions.mechanism: Can raise imipramine/desipramine levels, increasing side effects and cardiac risk.
interactions.action: Consider lower imipramine doses, slower titration, and therapeutic drug monitoring in select cases; watch for toxicity.

interactions.interactant: Alcohol and other CNS depressants (sedating antihistamines, benzodiazepines, sleep meds, muscle relaxants)
interactions.mechanism: Additive sedation, impaired coordination, accidents, falls—especially early in treatment.
interactions.action: Avoid or minimize. If combined, use the lowest effective doses and caution about driving/operating machinery.

interactions.interactant: Medications that can affect heart rhythm or blood pressure
interactions.mechanism: Higher risk of arrhythmias, conduction problems, or severe hypotension in vulnerable patients.
interactions.action: Review cardiac history, consider baseline ECG in higher-risk patients, and monitor closely with dose increases.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Suicidality and clinical worsening: monitor closely early in treatment (especially first 1–2 months) and during dose increases/decreases; involve family/caregivers when possible.
Mental status: agitation, insomnia, irritability, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania/mania—especially in younger patients and those with bipolar risk.
Cardiac monitoring: assess cardiac history; consider baseline ECG and repeat with dose increases in higher-risk patients (older adults, high doses, preexisting cardiovascular disease).
Blood pressure and pulse: monitor for orthostatic hypotension and tachycardia during initiation and titration.
Anticholinergic side effects: constipation severity, urinary retention, blurred vision, confusion—especially in older adults.
Sedation and functional impairment: daytime sleepiness, driving safety, fall risk.
Serum sodium: monitor in at-risk patients (older adults, diuretic use, low body weight, severe illness) and with dose adjustments.
Weight and BMI: track changes over time, especially with long-term use.
Blood glucose: monitor in patients with diabetes or metabolic vulnerability.
CBC: consider if symptoms of infection occur (fever, sore throat) due to rare hematologic toxicity.

Therapeutic drug monitoring (select cases): trough levels just before the next dose; combined imipramine + desipramine therapeutic range commonly referenced as 175–300 ng/mL; alert levels above ~300 ng/mL may signal toxicity risk.

special_populations.pregnancy: Outcome data exist for TCAs including imipramine, but results vary and confounding is common. If someone is stable on imipramine and it’s working, continuation during pregnancy can be considered through shared decision-making, weighing relapse risk against medication risk. TCAs are generally not first-line for treatment-naive pregnant patients; use the lowest effective dose of a single agent and monitor closely. Physiologic changes in late pregnancy may alter levels; therapeutic drug monitoring can be considered in select cases.
special_populations.lactation: Imipramine and desipramine appear in breast milk. Infant serum levels are often low or undetectable in small reports, but monitoring is recommended for sedation and poor feeding. The manufacturer discourages breastfeeding on imipramine; however, clinical practice may support continuation in a stable, effectively treated parent when benefits outweigh risks and breastfeeding goals are considered.
special_populations.pediatric: Imipramine is not approved for pediatric depression; it is approved for nocturnal enuresis in children ≥6 years. Pediatric psychiatric use carries higher cardiac concern and requires careful risk assessment and monitoring (including ECG considerations in some cases).
special_populations.geriatric: Avoid if possible (Beers Criteria): strong anticholinergic burden, sedation, and orthostatic hypotension increase risk of confusion, falls, fractures, and hyponatremia. If used despite risks, start very low, titrate slowly, and monitor closely (blood pressure, cognition, falls, sodium, ECG when indicated).
special_populations.renal_impairment: No formal manufacturer adjustment; limited unchanged urinary excretion. Use caution in renal impairment and monitor for side effects, especially in medically complex patients.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: No formal manufacturer adjustment, but use caution due to hepatic metabolism. Some experts reduce initial and maintenance doses by ~50% in hepatic impairment and titrate slowly with close monitoring.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed; not significantly affected by food
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Imipramine: ~8 to 21 hours (mean ~16-17 hours in adults); desipramine (active metabolite): ~22 to 28 hours
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic, primarily via CYP2D6 to desipramine (active) and other metabolites

dosing.titration: Imipramine dosing is usually slow and intentional. Some people are sensitive to TCAs, so starting low (even 10 mg at night) and titrating gradually can reduce early dropout from side effects. For depression, doses may end up in the 100–300 mg/day range depending on setting and tolerability. Bedtime dosing is common because the medication can be sedating.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: If you’ve been on imipramine for more than a few weeks, don’t stop abruptly. A gradual taper lowers the chance of withdrawal symptoms and helps us catch relapse early.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Imipramine is a tricyclic antidepressant used for {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:major depression}. In psychiatry today, it’s usually a “later-line” option because it’s effective but comes with a bigger side-effect and safety profile than SSRIs/SNRIs—especially anticholinergic effects, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, and cardiac rhythm risk. Some clinicians also use TCAs like imipramine off-label for panic symptoms when other treatments haven’t helped, but it’s not a quick fix—benefit builds over weeks.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (unipolar)}: Depressed mood, loss of interest, sleep/appetite changes, low energy, impaired concentration
Depression with prominent anxiety or agitation: Sometimes chosen when the symptom mix fits and other meds haven’t worked
{link:condition:panic-disorder:Panic symptoms} (off-label): May help in select patients over weeks, with careful monitoring
off_label: Insomnia as a secondary target (sedation at bedtime is sometimes used, but not the primary purpose)

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: My mouth felt like the Sahara. I couldn’t stop drinking water.
I was sleepy and kind of foggy—like my brain was wearing a hoodie.
I stood up and got that whoa-I-need-to-sit-down dizziness.
items.note: Early side effects often show up before mood improves. That doesn’t mean it won’t work—but it does mean you need a plan for tolerability.

quotes: Around week two I realized I wasn’t crying every day.
It wasn’t a sudden flip—more like the heaviness got lighter over time.
My anxiety stopped running the whole show, but it took a few weeks.
items.note: Improvements typically build over 4–6 weeks (sometimes longer), especially if you’re titrating slowly.

quotes: At bedtime it knocked me out… but mornings were rough.
I slept, but I felt hungover the next day.
It helped me stay asleep—just had to find the right dose.
items.note: Sedation can help sleep, but next-day grogginess and dizziness are common—especially during dose increases.

quotes: My heart felt weird—like pounding or fluttering.
I felt confused and off-balance, like my body wasn’t cooperating.
I got constipated in a way that felt almost impressive (not in a good way).
items.note: Palpitations, fainting, severe dizziness, confusion, urinary retention, or severe constipation aren’t “push through it” symptoms—those are call-your-clinician symptoms.

sections.intro: Imipramine has a very “TCA feel.” Some people love it. Some people bail fast. Here’s what tends to show up:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Imipramine doesn’t work like a benzo. You don’t take it and feel calm in an hour. This is a slow-build antidepressant with week-by-week change.
key_points: First few days: Side effects may show up before benefits (dry mouth, constipation, sedation, dizziness)
1–2 weeks: Early antidepressant effects may start to show (subtle shifts in sleep, energy, mood reactivity)
4–6 weeks: More complete mood benefit is common, especially after dose titration
Panic/anxiety symptoms (when used): Early changes may appear around ~2 weeks, with continued gains through 4–6+ weeks
Half-life: Imipramine averages ~16–17 hours in adults; the active metabolite (desipramine) lasts longer (~22–28 hours)

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Imipramine is a proven antidepressant, but it’s not commonly the first pick today because the tradeoffs can be steep: anticholinergic side effects, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, and higher cardiac risk than many newer antidepressants. When people tolerate it and the dose is optimized, it can be genuinely effective—especially in treatment-resistant patterns where several first-line options have failed. The key is respecting the medication: slow titration, safety screening, and close monitoring early on and during dose changes.
sections.clinical_details: Clinical practice often uses conservative starts (sometimes as low as 10 mg nightly in sensitive patients) with gradual increases every few days to weekly, aiming for symptom improvement while minimizing side effects. Full antidepressant response commonly requires several weeks at a therapeutic dose, and dose limits are influenced by tolerability, age, comorbidities, drug interactions, and cardiac risk. Therapeutic drug monitoring (imipramine + desipramine levels) can be helpful in select patients, especially at higher doses or when response is unclear.

patient_counseling: If you’re 24 or younger (or your loved one is), take the boxed warning seriously: we monitor more closely early on and during dose changes.
Call urgently if suicidal thoughts spike, depression suddenly worsens, or you develop intense agitation, insomnia, irritability, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania, or mania.
Stand up slowly. Hydrate. If you’re fainting or near-fainting, that’s not normal—tell your prescriber.
Dry mouth and constipation are common; urinary retention (can’t pee) is an urgent problem.
Don’t drive until you know how sedating it is for you.
Tell your prescriber about heart disease, fainting history, glaucoma risk, urinary issues, seizures, and all other meds/supplements.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Imipramine can be effective, but it has a high side-effect load compared with many newer antidepressants—especially anticholinergic symptoms (dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention), sedation, and orthostatic hypotension. Cardiac effects and confusion/falls are key concerns in older adults and at higher doses.

sections.intro: Imipramine has multiple interaction pathways: it’s strongly affected by CYP2D6 metabolism, it adds to sedation, and it can raise serotonin syndrome risk when stacked with other serotonergic agents. It also has meaningful cardiac interaction risk with certain meds.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’ve been on imipramine for more than a few weeks, don’t stop abruptly. A gradual taper lowers the chance of withdrawal symptoms and helps us catch relapse early.
key_points: If treatment lasted ≥4 weeks: taper gradually over ~2–4 weeks to reduce withdrawal symptoms and monitor for returning depression/anxiety.
If treatment lasted 2–3 weeks: taper over ~1–2 weeks is often reasonable.
If treatment lasted <2 weeks: tapering is often not necessary (but individual situations vary).
Go slower (≥4 weeks) if: you’ve had withdrawal symptoms before, you’re on higher doses, or you’re sensitive to dose changes.
If withdrawal symptoms become intolerable: return to the prior dose and taper more gradually.
Long-term treatment (>6 months): some patients do better with a very slow taper (sometimes months) if they’re prone to discontinuation symptoms.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Imipramine dosing is usually slow and intentional. Some people are sensitive to TCAs, so starting low (even 10 mg at night) and titrating gradually can reduce early dropout from side effects. For depression, doses may end up in the 100–300 mg/day range depending on setting and tolerability. Bedtime dosing is common because the medication can be sedating.

adult.depression_initial: 25 to 50 mg/day PO in divided doses or as a single bedtime dose (some experts start 10 mg nightly in sensitive patients)
adult.depression_titration: Increase by 25 to 50 mg/day at intervals of at least 1 week based on response and tolerability (some experts titrate every 3 to 4 days in very small steps when needed)
adult.depression_typical: 100 to 300 mg/day PO (individualize; outpatient doses often end up lower than inpatient dosing)
adult.depression_max: Up to 300 mg/day PO (higher doses increase side effect and cardiac risk; requires careful monitoring)
adult.bedtime: May be given as a single bedtime dose when sedation is helpful; otherwise divided dosing can improve tolerability
adult.panic_initial: 10 to 25 mg PO at bedtime in sensitive patients; titrate slowly based on response and tolerability

sections.simple_explanation: Imipramine is a week-by-week medication. Starting low helps your body adjust to sedation, dry mouth, constipation, and dizziness. The goal is to find the lowest dose that improves mood and anxiety without making you feel foggy, faint, or medically unsafe.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Imipramine is not usually the first choice in pregnancy or breastfeeding if someone is treatment-naive, but it may be continued in select patients who are already stable on it—because uncontrolled depression is also risky. In older adults (65+), imipramine is generally a “avoid if possible” medication due to strong anticholinergic effects, sedation, and orthostatic hypotension.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Imipramine is traditionally understood to work by blocking reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine—so more of those signals stay available in the brain. But TCAs don’t stop there: they also hit other receptors (including histamine and muscarinic receptors), which is a big reason the side effects can feel so “physical” (sedation, dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, dizziness). Over time, downstream receptor changes and signaling adaptations likely contribute to the antidepressant effect.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Imipramine is a classic antidepressant with real efficacy—but it’s usually not first-line in modern psychiatry because the safety/side-effect burden is heavier than many newer options. Where it can still make sense: treatment-resistant depression after multiple first-line trials, specific patient histories where a TCA previously worked well, or carefully selected cases where symptom pattern and past response justify the tradeoffs. If panic symptoms are part of the picture, it may help for some people, but it’s typically an off-label, specialist-style move due to tolerability and cardiac considerations.

faqs.q: What is imipramine used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: In psychiatry, imipramine is mainly used to treat unipolar major depressive disorder. Some clinicians also use it off-label for panic symptoms in select cases, but it’s not a first-line panic medication today because it has more side effects and more cardiac monitoring considerations than many newer antidepressants.

faqs.q: How long does imipramine take to work?
faqs.a: It’s a weeks-not-hours medication. Some people notice early changes in 1–2 weeks, but the fuller antidepressant effect usually builds over 4–6 weeks—especially after the dose is gradually increased to a therapeutic range.

faqs.q: Does imipramine help anxiety or panic right away?
faqs.a: No. It doesn’t work like a benzodiazepine. If it helps panic symptoms, it’s because of gradual antidepressant/anxiolytic effects that build over weeks. Early on, some people actually feel more jittery or activated before things settle—so monitoring matters.

faqs.q: Why is imipramine not a first-choice antidepressant anymore?
faqs.a: Because it’s effective but “heavy.” Imipramine commonly causes anticholinergic side effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, urinary retention), sedation, and orthostatic hypotension. It also has more cardiac risk than many newer antidepressants, especially at higher doses or in older adults.

faqs.q: What are the biggest safety concerns with imipramine?
faqs.a: The big three are: (1) the antidepressant boxed warning about suicidal thinking/behavior in people 24 and younger early in treatment and during dose changes, (2) cardiac rhythm/conduction risk (especially with heart disease, higher doses, or overdose), and (3) strong anticholinergic and blood pressure effects that can cause confusion, urinary retention, severe constipation, dizziness, and falls.

Yes, it can trigger mania or hypomania in people with bipolar disorder or bipolar vulnerability—like many antidepressants. If someone has a history of mania/hypomania or strong bipolar risk factors, imipramine monotherapy is usually avoided, and careful screening is important before starting.

faqs.q: What should I do if I feel more suicidal after starting imipramine?
faqs.a: Treat it as urgent. Contact your prescriber right away, and if you’re in danger or can’t stay safe, go to the ER or call emergency services. The risk is highest early in treatment and during dose changes—this is exactly why close monitoring and involving a trusted support person can be lifesaving.

It can be very sedating—especially early and after dose increases. Many people take it at night for that reason, but some still feel next-day grogginess or brain fog. Don’t drive until you know how it affects you.

faqs.q: What medications should not be mixed with imipramine?
faqs.a: MAOIs are the big hard no—you need a 14-day washout on either side. Caution is also needed with other serotonergic medications (risk of serotonin syndrome), strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (can raise imipramine levels), and sedatives/alcohol (worsen sedation and falls). Always review your full med list with the prescriber.

faqs.q: How do you taper off imipramine safely?
faqs.a: If you’ve taken it for 4+ weeks, taper gradually over about 2–4 weeks (or longer if you’re sensitive). If withdrawal symptoms hit hard, the usual move is to return to the previous dose and taper more slowly. If you’ve been on it long-term, a slower taper over months may be better for some people.

faqs.q: Is imipramine safe in older adults?
faqs.a: Often, no. In patients 65 and older, imipramine is generally considered a medication to avoid when possible because it can cause confusion, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, and falls—and it has strong anticholinergic burden. If it’s used anyway, it should be with very cautious dosing and close monitoring.
